title: A Harvest for the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Zephyrine Whitlock arrives in the drowned-harvest village of Marrowfen to record its songs, only to find the locals fall silent whenever the church bell is mentioned—a bell melted down in 1911 that begins ringing again each dusk. As Zephyrine documents the phenomenon, they discover the village has been feeding its dead to the bell for a century in exchange for impossible harvests, and that the song's missing last verse is a contract awaiting a new voice. When the bell chooses Zephyrine as its next singer, they must choose between belonging to Marrowfen's found family of the marked and breaking the cycle—by singing the last verse alone, giving the bell their own name, and freeing the village at the cost of being remembered by no one. In the end, the village forgets Zephyrine entirely, yet a child hums an unfamiliar tune at the harvest feast: the last verse, sung wrong, sung free.
about_author: J. M. Hartwell is the pen name of a former archivist of oral histories who spent a decade recording dying dialects across the English fens. Their fiction blends fieldwork's quiet dread with a folklorist's tenderness for the voices history tries to erase.

chapters.title: The Village That Wouldn't Repeat Itself
chapters.summary: Zephyrine Whitlock, POV. Arriving in Marrowfen with recording equipment and a grant deadline, Zephyrine is charmed by the harvest preparations but unsettled when every villager refuses to sing any song twice, claiming a second singing 'calls something back.' The emotional beat is wary curiosity—the folklorist's thrill at genuine taboo, shadowed by the villagers' too-uniform smiles.

chapters.title: Ink as a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. In the inn, Zephyrine transcribes the one song coaxed from old Tam Rooker and reflects on why documentation feels sacred to them—a childhood of being overlooked, made bearable by writing things down so they existed somewhere. Beat: establishing Zephyrine's loneliness and their belief that being recorded is a form of love.

chapters.title: A Bell with No Bell
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. At dusk a bell rings from the roofless church tower, though the tower holds nothing; the parish record confirms the bell was melted for scrap in 1911. Villagers hurry indoors, and the innkeeper's daughter Merrin whispers that you must never count the tolls. Beat: the first hard fracture in Zephyrine's rational worldview.

chapters.title: The Marked
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. Zephyrine notices a faint ring of scar tissue at the collarbones of certain villagers—Merrin, Tam, the blacksmith's widow—and realizes the marked ones are those who once sang along. Merrin, half-drunk on cider courage, admits the bell takes a voice every generation. Beat: dread mixed with the first flicker of intimacy between Zephyrine and Merrin.

chapters.title: Fieldwork Among the Willing
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. Merrin shows Zephyrine the harvest fields that never fail, even in drought years, and the ledger of names in the church vestry—every marked villager, every 'given' voice since 1911. She wants Zephyrine's outsider eyes to see what the villagers cannot. Beat: complicity; Merrin chooses to betray the village's silence.

chapters.title: The Song with Four Verses
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. Tam Rooker, dying and unafraid, sings the harvest song's first three verses and refuses the fourth: 'The last verse isn't sung, lad. It's owed.' Zephyrine records it anyway and hears, on playback, a fourth voice beneath Tam's that no one else can hear. Beat: the horror of the archive becoming a haunted object.

chapters.title: What the Tape Keeps
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. Reviewing recordings at night, Zephyrine isolates the fourth voice—an old woman singing the missing verse in a dialect dead a century. When Zephyrine plays it aloud, every marked villager within earshot clutches their scarred collarbones and the bell tolls once, off schedule. Beat: Zephyrine realizes documentation is not neutral; the tape is a summons.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Ledger
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Merrin, alternating POV. They break into the vestry and read the ledger's final page: a blank line awaiting the next name, and a note in 1911 copperplate—'the bell keeps what is sung to it, and the fields keep the village.' Beat: the machinery of the bargain revealed; power sustained by sacrifice.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. The village prepares the feast with desperate festivity, and Zephyrine is publicly welcomed, toasted, claimed—given a seat, a mug, a family's warmth they've never had. Merrin watches Zephyrine glow under the belonging and fears what the welcome is for. Beat: found family offered with poisoned roots; tenderness laced with dread.

chapters.title: The Choosing
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. At the feast's height the bell rings thirteen times and every marked villager turns to look at Zephyrine. The vicar explains gently: the bell has heard Zephyrine's recordings, has heard them sing along to Tam's verses while transcribing. The blank line in the ledger is already writing itself. Beat: betrayal of the self by the self—the archivist's devotion weaponized.

chapters.title: Run, or Root
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. Merrin begs Zephyrine to flee before the new moon; Zephyrine, shaken, discovers their car dead, the lane hedged with hawthorn that wasn't there yesterday. The village doesn't imprison them—it simply makes leaving unthinkable, and Zephyrine catches themselves wanting to stay. Beat: the seduction of belonging as a cage.

chapters.title: Voices Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. Sleepless, Zephyrine hears singing through the inn's floorboards and finds the cellar hung with wax cylinders and reel-to-reels—a century of the given voices, still singing, preserved perfectly. Among them, the 1911 voice sings the last verse, and Zephyrine, listening, realizes they can now hum it without ever having learned it. Beat: contamination; knowledge as infection.

chapters.title: The Widow's Confession
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. The blacksmith's widow, oldest of the marked, tells the truth: in 1911 the village starved, the vicar sold their voices to the bell, and the harvests have been bought with a singer every generation. She was given in 1968; she remembers nothing of her old life but the singing felt like home. Beat: grief for the complicit; the village as victim and perpetrator at once.

chapters.title: What Documentation Cannot Do
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. Zephyrine tries to break the contract by destroying the recordings, but the voices persist in their head, and the ledger line fills in letter by letter with their own name. The theme crystallizes: you cannot archive your way out of being claimed. Beat: despair; the failure of Zephyrine's one true faith.

chapters.title: Merrin's Verse
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. Merrin reveals her own secret: she was marked as a child, meant to be given at eighteen, and her mother took her place. She has spent her life humming fragments of the last verse, trying to learn it wrong on purpose, to spoil it. Beat: hope through imperfection—the idea that a song sung wrongly loses its power.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Bargain
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. The vicar offers Zephyrine a choice framed as mercy: sing willingly and the village prospers another century, and Zephyrine will be remembered as a saint of Marrowfen; refuse and the bell will take a child instead. Beat: the corrupting logic of power—sacrifice dressed as virtue, the exact temptation the village has always accepted.

chapters.title: New Moon
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Merrin, alternating POV. The night of the choosing arrives; the whole village gathers in the roofless church, and the empty tower fills with a bell of sound and moonlight. Zephyrine, scar tissue blooming at their own collarbones, stands before the ledger. Beat: terrible calm before the climax; Zephyrine at last unafraid because they have a plan.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, POV. Climax. Instead of singing the verse as the bell demands, Zephyrine sings it alone—unaccompanied, deliberately wrong, with their own name woven into it as the giver—so the contract binds only themselves. The bell cracks like ice on a pond; a century of voices pours out of the tower and disperses like starlings. Beat: catharsis; power broken not by refusal but by rewriting the terms.

chapters.title: Aftermath of a Bell
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. The village wakes to ordinary fields, ordinary hunger, ordinary weather—and to freedom they did not ask for. Some mourn the bargain; the widow weeps with relief. Merrin searches the crowd for Zephyrine and cannot recall their face. Beat: the cost made flesh; grief for someone who is not gone but erased.

chapters.title: The Blank Page
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. In the vestry, the ledger's last line holds Zephyrine's name fading like breath off glass; the wax cylinders in the cellar are blank. Merrin finds Zephyrine's field notebook, intact, and reads their own name in it—proof she mattered to someone who no longer exists to her. Beat: mourning and gratitude entangled; the archive outliving the archivist.

chapters.title: A Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. At the harvest feast, Merrin teaches the villagers the harvest song—all four verses—and for the first time in a century they sing it twice, badly, laughing. The scarred villagers find the marks have faded to pale lines. Beat: restoration; belonging rebuilt on choice instead of debt.

chapters.title: The Humming Child
chapters.summary: Merrin, POV. Resolution. A child at the feast hums a tune no one taught her—the last verse, sung wrong, sung free—and Merrin, recording it on Zephyrine's abandoned machine, whispers a thank-you to a name she can't remember. In the last line, somewhere on the fen road, a traveler with no past hums the same tune walking toward a town that has never heard of Marrowfen. Beat: bittersweet grace; memory lost, song survived.
